literal: Let sulk oh that, bright jewel, we to beg; let lengthen oh that, night.
translation: Let the brightly jeweled woman feign anger so I may plead with her, and let the night stretch on to give us time.
modern: ஒளிரும் அணிகலன்களை அணிந்தவள் என்னோடு ஊடல் கொள்வாளாக; அவளிடம் நான் கெஞ்சி இரந்து நிற்பதற்காக இந்த இரவு இன்னும் நீள்வதாக.
explanation: The speaker expresses a deep delight in the lover's feigned quarrel. He wishes that the woman, described metonymically by her bright jewels, would continue to sulk so that he can have the pleasure of pleading with her. To fully enjoy this sweet process of appeasing her, he wishes for the night to stretch on and last longer. The optative verbs 'ūṭuka' (let her sulk) and 'nīṭuka' (let it lengthen) highlight his active desire for this playful conflict and the time to resolve it.
